title: Artificial intelligence and cyber threats to peace
summary: Security Council practice on cyberattacks on hospitals and power grids, ransomware, human control of nuclear launch decisions and how far the Council itself should act on AI.

tags.infrastructure_protection: Protects hospitals, power grids and other key infrastructure from cyberattack
tags.state_responsibility: Makes States answerable for cyberattacks launched from their territory

resolution.title: Artificial intelligence and cyber threats to international peace and security

preambular.text: Recalling the purposes and principles of the Charter of the United Nations, and the Security Council's primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace and security,

Recalling that Member States have agreed, in reports endorsed by the General Assembly, that international law, including the Charter, applies to the use of information and communications technologies,
Noting the Council's open debates on artificial intelligence in July 2023 and September 2025, and on threats in cyberspace in June 2024,
Noting that digital technologies bring real benefits to health care, education and economies, alongside new risks,

operative.text: Calls upon all States to refrain from cyberattacks on hospitals, power grids, water systems and other critical infrastructure, and to protect such infrastructure on their own territory;
Calls upon every State to take reasonable steps to stop ransomware and other cyberattacks being launched from its territory, and to investigate and prosecute those responsible;

Calls upon nuclear-armed States to adopt and publish national policies that keep a human in control of every decision to use nuclear weapons, including where artificial intelligence supports early warning or command systems;
Encourages all Member States to take part in United Nations discussions on the military use of artificial intelligence;

Requests the Secretary-General to brief the Council regularly on how artificial intelligence and cyber threats affect international peace and security, drawing on the General Assembly's cyber processes rather than repeating them;
Requests the Secretary-General to report on how artificial intelligence is used to spread false information that fuels armed conflict, and on steps States can take to counter it.

cards.text: Demands that States immediately stop all cyberattacks on hospitals and power grids, and decides that the Council will keep the matter under review;
Encourages States to share good practice on protecting hospitals and water systems from cyberattack, on a voluntary basis;
Urges States to respond promptly when another State asks for help because its critical infrastructure is under cyberattack, and to cooperate in investigations;
Encourages nuclear-armed States to discuss, in whatever forum they choose, how human judgement is kept in decisions about the use of nuclear weapons;
Calls upon nuclear-armed States to declare that artificial intelligence will never make or carry out a decision to use nuclear weapons without human approval;
Requests States to report voluntarily to the Secretary-General on the steps they take against cyberattacks launched from their territory, without any finding of blame;
Requests the Secretary-General to include in his briefings advice on how United Nations talks on military AI could inform the Council's work, without creating a new body;
Urges States to support independent fact-checking and media literacy, so that false AI-made content is less likely to inflame armed conflict;

events.title: An expert briefs delegates on Council briefings
events.body: A technical expert gives delegates a closed briefing on how regular Council briefings on cyber threats could work alongside the General Assembly's own processes.
events.teaches: The Council and the General Assembly have different roles, and good drafting avoids repeating work done elsewhere.

events.title: Delegates ask what human control really means
events.body: In consultations, delegates ask what human control of a launch decision would require in practice. Supporters of the clause press the point.
events.teaches: Words in resolutions get tested for precise meaning, and vague terms are often where agreement or disagreement hides.

events.title: A permanent member's capital sends new instructions
events.body: A permanent member's capital sends fresh instructions, and its delegation asks for a pause to study them. Your plans for this turn must wait.
events.teaches: The five permanent members can veto, so their capitals' instructions matter to every deal in the Council.

events.title: Closed consultations run long
events.body: Closed consultations overrun their time and delegates drift away to other meetings. Reaching people is harder this turn.
events.teaches: Much Council work happens in closed consultations, and time is one of the scarcest things a delegation has.

events.title: Elected members agree to speak together
events.body: Several elected members meet and agree to speak with one voice. They credit you with clarifying the text, and your standing grows.
events.teaches: Elected members have no veto, but acting together gives them a louder voice in the Council.

events.title: A regional group meets on the draft
events.body: A regional group meets to consider the draft and invites you to explain it. Delegates who have worked with them hear you out.
events.teaches: Members often consult their regional groups, and trust built there carries into Council votes.

author: Claude Sonnet (delegated), 4 Nov 2026; to be checked by B. Gough
